senses.definition: A people scattered from a homeland who keep a tie to it, and the fact of that scattering. The word carries the history of why they left, which is usually not by choice.
senses.caution: The weight is the whole risk. Stretched to any dispersed group — ex-colleagues of a firm, alumni of a team, people who left a project — it sounds glib to anyone whose family actually belongs to one, and that person is more often in the room than not. If you mean a network of former employees, say alumni network.
senses.example: The growth story there is remittances — money moving back through the diaspora — not domestic demand.

cues.text: A friend describes a wedding where everyone's parents left the same country decades ago and almost nobody has been back.
You are explaining why one neighbourhood has three bakeries selling the same bread from one small region.
You are reading about a language kept alive abroad long after it faded where it began.
You are explaining to a colleague that a country's economy runs largely on money sent home by people living overseas.

distractors: The arrival of newcomers into one country, counted at the border and argued about in its politics.
The blending of two cultures into a third that belongs wholly to neither, visible first in the food and in the language.
A community that shares a trade rather than an origin, held together by the work itself and by the annual conference where its members recognise each other and then go home again.

A group that has withdrawn from the society around it on purpose and keeps its own rules inside a boundary it drew itself. What defines it is the choosing, and the boundary is maintained from the inside.

The movement of people out of the countryside and into cities inside one country, which reshapes both ends of it within a generation: labour arrives where the work is and the villages empty out behind it. It is measured by economists more often than it is remembered by families.
